## The problem

Greater Boston's bus network carries the region's most transit-dependent riders
on some of its slowest and least reliable services. Black bus riders in Boston
spend roughly **64 more hours a year** in transit than white riders.

Over a weekend at the MIT Policy Hackathon, my teammates
[Anushri Gade and Rahul Tejannavar]{.nowrap} and I asked three questions: which
routes does that penalty fall hardest on, can it be fixed without a capital
megaproject, and what would fixing it cost?

## How we found the corridors

Ranking routes by need alone rewards lightly-used shuttles through very poor
neighbourhoods. Ranking by ridership alone rewards busy routes through affluent
ones. We needed something that asked a blunter question: **where are the most
equity-weighted riders?**

So we built a **Transit Dependence Index** for every route in the network —
population-weighted shares of zero-vehicle households, residents below 200% of
the poverty line, non-white residents, and transit commuters, measured within an
800 metre walkshed of every stop and normalised against the system average. Then
we multiplied it by ridership.

![Routes 28, 23 and 66 sit furthest out on both axes at once — that is what the product picks up.](/images/mbta/figures/fig02_equity_volume_scatter.png){.rounded fig-alt="Scatter plot of transit dependence index against weekday boardings"}

Three routes — **28, 23 and 66** — came out first, second and third in the
entire MBTA bus network. Then we checked what service those riders actually get.

![](/images/mbta/figures/fig03_service_deficit.png){.rounded fig-alt="Bar chart of peak runtime and unreliability by route"}

All three run longer than the median peak runtime. Route 66 takes nearly **49
minutes** at peak with the worst on-time performance in the group.

> The more you depend on the bus, the more you are punished by slow and
> unreliable service.

## Why it's a labour-market problem

Using LEHD LODES employment microdata, we found the corridor is itself a major
job centre — over 69,000 health and social assistance jobs sit inside it — and
yet only about **one quarter** of the jobs held by corridor residents are located
there. Residents work at more than 12,000 distinct workplace blocks.

![](/images/mbta/figures/fig06_sector_composition.png){.rounded fig-alt="Corridor residents versus rest of Massachusetts by employment sector"}

Most riders are passing through to somewhere else, usually via a rail transfer.
That reframes a local transit intervention as a regional access problem, and it
is the finding the recommendation rests on.

## What it costs, and what it returns

Not a megaproject. Dedicated lanes on congested segments, transit signal
priority, queue jumps at bottlenecks, far-side stops and stop consolidation —
tools Boston already deploys, at roughly $0.5M a mile. Ten miles of treatment,
**$6.5 million** all in.

The model keeps three benefit buckets separate, because they are not the same
kind of money:

| Bucket | Per year | In the payback? |
|---|---:|:--:|
| Net operating savings, after reinvesting half into service | $3.16M | ✅ |
| New rail fare revenue from better bus–rail feeding | $0.56M | ✅ |
| Rider time value (1.23M hours at $10–20/hr) | $12.3–24.5M | ❌ |

Rider time is a societal benefit, not agency cash. Mixing the two into a payback
figure is how cost-benefit analyses get dismissed by the people who have to sign
them off. So payback and NPV use the first two buckets only — and it still
clears in **1.7 years**.

![](/images/mbta/figures/fig04_payback.png){.rounded fig-alt="Cumulative discounted net benefit crossing zero at 1.7 years"}

### Does it survive pessimism?

The interesting question isn't what the model says at the central case. It's how
far you have to push the assumptions before the recommendation breaks.

![](/images/mbta/figures/fig05_speed_sensitivity.png){.rounded fig-alt="Payback period and NPV across runtime reduction scenarios"}

The package pays back inside five years even at a **5% runtime reduction** —
half the bottom of the range documented for comparable bus-priority projects.

## A note on what came after

The original analysis notebooks were lost after the event. What survived was the
memo, the deck, and a working document with the intermediate tables and part of
the original GeoPandas code.

Rather than let the work disappear, I rebuilt it as a
[documented, tested Python package](https://github.com/sahilmittal-policy/mbta-equity-corridors).
The cost-benefit model is verified — it reproduces every published figure, and
42 tests pin it there so a refactor can't quietly change the answer. The spatial
pipeline is reconstructed but not re-executed, and the repository says so
plainly.

It also documents three things that don't reconcile, including a composite index
whose published formula doesn't reproduce its published value. That index is
implemented **as published**, and the repository reports what it yields rather
than back-fitting to the reported number.
